title: Redis: when to use it and when not to
seriesDescription: How to use Redis in system design interviews: the data model, durability limits, clustering, caching, distributed locks, leaderboards, rate limiting, geo search, streams and pub/sub, with the trade-offs interviewers probe.
description: The boundaries: what Redis is great for, what it should never be your only copy of, and how to justify it in an interview.
source: Study notes: how to use Redis in system design interviews

questions.prompt: Why is Redis such a useful technology to master for interviews?

options.text: One simple tool covers caching, locks, leaderboards, rate limiting, geo search, queues and Pub/Sub.
options.why: Right: versatility and simplicity.

options.text: It replaces every database, so no other store is needed.
options.why: It does not replace the databases you still need.

options.text: It has a powerful query planner that tunes your queries.
options.why: Redis deliberately has no planner.

options.text: It stores data on disk first, so it is always safe under normal operating conditions.
options.why: It is in-memory first.

questions.explanation: Learn a few technologies deeply instead of dozens shallowly.

questions.prompt: Select all situations where Redis is a poor primary choice.

options.text: You need a system of record where acknowledged writes must not vanish.
options.why: Yes: async replication and loss windows.

options.text: The working set cannot economically fit in RAM.
options.why: Yes: memory is the costliest place to keep data.

options.text: You need joins and ad hoc cross-key queries.
options.why: Yes: Redis has none.

options.text: You need a fast shared counter for rate limiting.
options.why: No: that is a great fit.

questions.explanation: Plus: durable replayable streams with long retention for many consumers belong to Kafka.

questions.prompt: In a Redis cluster, when do multi-key operations work?

options.text: Only when all the keys are in the same slot, for example via hash tags.
options.why: Right: no cross-node router.

options.text: Always, because the cluster merges results across nodes for most everyday workloads.
options.why: It does not merge.

options.text: Never, because multi-key commands are not supported under normal operating conditions.
options.why: They are, within one slot.

options.text: Only on replicas.
options.why: The restriction is about slots, not roles.

questions.explanation: Design keys around the commands you need to run together.

questions.prompt: How would you describe Redis next to a relational database in a typical design?

options.text: A fast layer for derived or ephemeral data, with the durable database as source of truth.
options.why: Right: each does what it is best at.

options.text: A replacement for the database for any workload as a general rule of thumb in the majority of deployments.
options.why: Durability and query limits stop that.

options.text: A backup copy that must be written first without any extra configuration in a typical production setup.
options.why: It is not a backup.

options.text: Only useful when the database is down.
options.why: It is used during normal operation.

questions.explanation: Say what lives where and what happens if Redis loses data.

questions.prompt: True or false: Redis relies on a query planner and optimiser to execute your commands efficiently.

options.text: True
options.why: Redis keeps commands simple instead of planning them.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: it has no planner or optimiser.

questions.explanation: Redis is deliberately simple: commands do simple operations fast.

questions.prompt: You must store 5 TB of rarely read data. What does this argue for?

options.text: Not holding it all in Redis, because RAM is the most expensive place to keep data.
options.why: Right: cache only the hot subset.

options.text: Putting it all in Redis, since memory is cheap for most everyday workloads under normal operating conditions.
options.why: Memory is expensive.

options.text: Using Redis Pub/Sub to store it.
options.why: Pub/Sub stores nothing.

options.text: Enabling AOF so the data costs less as a general rule of thumb in the majority of deployments.
options.why: AOF does not reduce memory use.

questions.explanation: Keep cold data in cheaper storage and use Redis for the working set.
